catalogue_metadata.scope_notes: This catalogue focuses on non-agentic structural, domain, and integration patterns. Agentic patterns (LLM loops, prompt contracts) are intentionally excluded as they are covered by a complementary agentic extractor.
analysis_limits: Only top-level source files under src/cas_runner and selected workflow validation scripts were analyzed. Detailed module internals beyond listed symbols were not inspected.
Evidence is based on file paths and symbols provided in the runtime input. Some patterns are inferred from file naming and import structure, but may require deeper code review for full validation.
The repository contains as-yet-unexplored submodules (e.g., cas-brain, cas-knowledge) that may host additional structural patterns not captured here.

system_map.overview: The system is a Python-based automation and governance platform for AI-assisted development workflows. It provides a CLI (cli.py) as the entry point, a runner (FlowRunner) that orchestrates execution flows, and a set of governance modules that manage compliance, action transitions, and health dashboards. LLM interactions are abstracted through a client interface (LiteLLMClient, MockLLMClient). The system also includes a bootstrap process that merges governance blocks and configuration into the workspace.

patterns.name: Transition Registry State Machine
patterns.summary: Encapsulates state transition logic in a dedicated registry that maps allowed transitions, enabling centralized validation and auditing.
patterns.intent: To manage the lifecycle of governance actions in a controlled, predictable manner without scattering transition logic across the codebase.
patterns.context: Governance actions need to move through defined states (e.g., pending, approved, rejected) with validation to prevent illegal transitions.
forces: Need for consistent state validation across different callers
Desire to avoid tight coupling between state transitions and business logic
Requirement for extendability to add new states or transitions
Need for auditability of transitions
patterns.solution: Implement a TransitionRegistry class that holds a map of valid transitions for each state. The GovernanceActionEngine uses this registry to validate and execute state changes, returning clear errors for invalid transitions.
implementation_signals: Class named TransitionRegistry in governance_action_engine.py
GovernanceActionEngine referencing the registry for state changes

benefits: Single source of truth for allowed transitions
costs: Requires initial design effort
May become complex if state machine grows
failure_modes: Registry not updated when states change

patterns.reuse_notes: This pattern can be reused for any entity lifecycle management within the domain.

patterns.name: Pydantic Domain Entity Modeling
patterns.summary: Use Pydantic models to define domain entities with validation, type safety, and serialization support, serving as the backbone for data consistency.
patterns.intent: To model domain entities and DTOs with minimal boilerplate while ensuring validation and structured data flow.
patterns.context: The system needs to represent governance findings, metrics, capabilities, and other domain objects that are passed between modules and persisted.
forces: Need for data validation to catch errors early
Requirement for type safety and IDE support
Ease of serialization to JSON/YAML
Need for schema evolution
patterns.solution: Define all domain models as Pydantic BaseModel subclasses, leveraging field validation, type coercion, and model serialization.
implementation_signals: Multiple model classes inheriting from Pydantic BaseModel in governance/models.py and steering/models.py
Enums used for constrained string values

costs: Requires dependency on Pydantic
Potential performance overhead for complex validation
failure_modes: Misuse of models for non-domain purposes

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply this pattern to any new domain entity following the same structure.

patterns.name: LLM Client Abstraction
patterns.summary: Define an interface (abstract base class) for LLM clients with concrete implementations (LiteLLMClient, MockLLMClient) to allow swapping providers or mock usage for testing.
patterns.intent: To decouple the application logic from the specific LLM provider, enabling testability and provider flexibility.
patterns.context: The system interacts with LLMs for various purposes; there is a need to run tests without calling external APIs and to switch providers if needed.
forces: Avoid hard dependency on a single LLM provider
Enable unit testing without API calls
Ease of adding new providers
Maintain consistent API for callers
patterns.solution: Create a client interface (e.g., LLMClient) with methods for completion/request. Provide real and mock implementations that conform to this interface.
implementation_signals: Files named litellm_client.py and mock_client.py in the llm directory
Both likely implement a common base class

costs: Extra abstraction layer
Potential feature-loss if interface too narrow
failure_modes: Interface not defined, leading to direct provider usage

patterns.reuse_notes: Consider using this pattern for any external service integration.

patterns.name: Compliance Engine Centralized Checker
patterns.summary: Encapsulate compliance checking logic in a dedicated engine that evaluates metrics and produces findings, providing a single point of compliance evaluation.
patterns.intent: To centralize compliance evaluation to ensure consistent and auditable checks across the system.
patterns.context: The system needs to enforce governance rules and track compliance health over time.
forces: Avoid code duplication in compliance checks
Need for consistent reporting and metrics
Ability to extend with new checks
patterns.solution: Create ComplianceEngine class that takes relevant domain data and returns ComplianceMetrics and ComplianceFinding objects, encapsulating all verification logic.
implementation_signals: ComplianceEngine class in compliance_engine.py
Methods for evaluating specific compliance aspects

costs: May be over-centralized if not modularized
Potential performance bottlenecks if complex checks
failure_modes: Circumvention of engine for ad-hoc checks

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any domain requiring systematic validation or rule checking.

patterns.name: Service Layer Pattern
patterns.summary: Introduce a service layer (e.g., GovernanceActionService) that orchestrates domain operations and provides a cohesive API to callers, decoupling the presentation from domain logic.
patterns.intent: To provide a clear boundary for business operations, encapsulating domain workflows and reducing dependencies on internal domain objects.
patterns.context: The GovernanceActionService likely mediates between the CLI/runner and the governance domain, executing actions with proper coordination.
forces: Need for clear separation between application and domain layers
Simplify client code by exposing high-level operations
Enable transaction management and audit logging
patterns.solution: Define service classes that own use-case logic, delegating to domain entities and engines. Clients interact only with the service layer.
implementation_signals: Presence of governance_action_service.py
CLI or runner references the service

costs: Additional layer may be overkill for small operations
Risk of over-abstraction

patterns.reuse_notes: Use for any complex workflow involving multiple domain objects.

patterns.name: Factory Method for Bootstrap
patterns.summary: Use a bootstrap function that creates and configures required components (e.g., merging governance blocks, settings) to initialize the workspace.
patterns.intent: To centralize initialization logic and allow customization of the setup process.
patterns.context: The system needs to set up a consistent workspace including governance block merging and symlink creation when first run or on updates.
forces: Avoid scattered initialization code
Need for idempotent and reproducible setup
Potential for extension without modifying main flow
patterns.solution: Implement a bootstrap function that orchestrates the creation of directories, symlinks, and merges of governance blocks using helper functions.
implementation_signals: Function named init_workspace or bootstrap in bootstrap.py
Helper functions like merge_cas_governance_block and _create_symlink_or_copy

costs: May become complex if too many variations
Hidden dependencies in global state
failure_modes: Failure in one step aborting entire setup

patterns.name: Health Calculation Strategy
patterns.summary: Encapsulate health scoring logic in dedicated functions (calculate_health, get_health_reasons) allowing for easy extension and testing.
patterns.intent: To compute a health indicator for the system from various metrics and provide human-readable reasons.
patterns.context: The dashboard needs to display system health based on governance metrics, possibly including LLM or execution health.
forces: Need for consistent health scoring
Ability to add new health factors
Separation from UI concerns
patterns.solution: Define pure functions that accept metrics and return a HealthStatus plus reasons, ensuring deterministic and testable health logic.
implementation_signals: Functions named calculate_health and get_health_reasons in health_model.py
Enum HealthStatus

benefits: Easy to extend with new metrics
costs: Potential over-simplification of complex health factors

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any system needing aggregated status scoring.

patterns.name: Workflow Validation Script
patterns.summary: Provide standalone validation scripts (e.g., validate_workflows.py) that verify CI/CD workflow configuration files for syntax and best-practice compliance.
patterns.intent: To automate the detection of common CI/CD misconfigurations in a repository, such as unpinned installers or unreachable dry runs.
patterns.context: The repository includes multiple GitHub workflows that should follow maintainability rules (e.g., no hardcoding, no unpinned actions). A dedicated script is used in CI to enforce these.
forces: Prevent regressions in workflow hygiene
Provide fast feedback in CI
Enforce consistent standards without manual review
patterns.solution: Create a Python script that reads YAML workflow files and runs specific checks (syntax, pinning, hardcoding, unreachable states) and exits with an error code if any fail.
implementation_signals: Functions like check_yaml_syntax, check_zero_hardcoding, check_no_unpinned_installers

benefits: Can be run locally or in CI
costs: Script maintenance required as standards evolve
May miss nuanced issues

patterns.reuse_notes: Adapt this pattern for other configuration file validation (e.g., docs, schemas).

patterns.name: Dependency Inversion via Interfaces
patterns.summary: Invert dependencies by depending on abstractions (interfaces) rather than concrete implementations, as exemplified by the LLM client abstraction.
patterns.intent: To decouple high-level policy from low-level detail implementations, enabling swapping and testing.
patterns.context: The runner depends on LLM clients but should not know concrete provider details.
forces: Enable test doubles
Avoid modification when providers change
Facilitate parallel development
patterns.solution: Define a client interface or abstract base class that the concrete clients implement. High-level modules depend on that interface.
implementation_signals: Multiple client classes in llm/ directory
Persistent use of a common interface in type hints

evidence.note: Concrete client, likely implements an interface

costs: Requires extra abstraction
Potential over-engineering if only one implementation
failure_modes: Using concrete types in high-level code

patterns.reuse_notes: Apply to any external service boundary.

patterns.name: Module Boundary Encapsulation
patterns.summary: Group related classes and functions into modules by responsibility (governance, llm, steering, dashboard) to maintain clear boundaries and easier navigation.
patterns.intent: To organize code so that each package has a single, well-defined purpose, facilitating maintenance and reducing cross-cutting changes.
patterns.context: The src/cas_runner directory contains subpackages for each major concern (governance, llm, steering, dashboard).
forces: Reduce coupling between unrelated concepts
Improve readability and onboarding
Enable independent testing and evolution
patterns.solution: Maintain a separation of concerns via directories: each containing models, services, and engines related to that domain.
implementation_signals: Presence of governance/, llm/, steering/, dashboard/ directories

costs: Fragmentation if over-modularized
Potential cyclic dependencies if boundaries not enforced

patterns.reuse_notes: Use consistent module naming conventions across the codebase.

patterns.name: Configuration Hardcoding Avoidance
patterns.summary: Avoid hardcoding environment-specific values (e.g., paths, version numbers) in workflows and code by using configuration files and environment variables.
patterns.intent: To improve portability and reduce maintenance burden by moving variable settings out of source code.
patterns.context: Validation script includes check_zero_hardcoding to enforce that no hardcoded numbers or values appear in workflow files.
forces: Promote reuse across environments
Simplify updates when dependencies change
Reduce errors from stale hardcoded values
patterns.solution: Use configuration files (e.g., YAML) or environment variables to manage settings, and enforce no hardcoding via linting/validation.
implementation_signals: Function check_zero_hardcoding in validation script
Presence of configuration file (execution-profile.yaml)

evidence.note: Configuration file used for runtime settings

costs: Configuration sprawl
Potential lack of discoverability

anti_patterns.name: Over-Centralized Engines
symptoms: Engines (ComplianceEngine, GovernanceActionEngine) becoming too large with many responsibilities
Multiple callers depending on a single engine, decreasing maintainability
suggested_remediation: Break down engines into smaller, focused components
Use composition and delegate to specialized services

anti_patterns.name: Missing LLM Client Interface
symptoms: LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient exist but no explicit common interface defined
Static type checking may fail to prevent misuse
suggested_remediation: Define a common abstract base class (e.g., LLMClient)
Ensure all clients inherit from it and use type hints with the base class

anti_patterns.name: Scattered Bootstrap Logic
symptoms: Bootstrap contains many helper functions (merge_claude_settings, _create_symlink_or_copy) suggesting complex procedural startup
impact: Hard to trace what happens during initialization
Testing becomes complex with many side effects
suggested_remediation: Modularize bootstrap into small, single-purpose classes

anti_patterns.name: Undefined Step Registry Interface
symptoms: No evidence of a formal Step registry or interface for flow steps
FlowRunner may handle steps imperatively, leading to code growth
impact: Difficulty extending the runner with new steps
Potential tight coupling between flow logic and step contexts
suggested_remediation: Define a Step interface and a registry mapping step names to classes
Use the registry to look up and execute steps dynamically

anti_patterns.name: Magic String Usage
symptoms: Presence of string literals for states, transition keys, or action types in governance modules
Hard-coded file paths in scripts (e.g., workflow files)
suggested_remediation: Use enums or constants for state names and action types

cross_cutting_concerns.name: Logging & Auditing
cross_cutting_concerns.description: Governance actions and compliance inspections should be logged for traceability. No explicit logging module was observed; likely handled through framework or standard library.

cross_cutting_concerns.name: Error Handling & Resilience
cross_cutting_concerns.description: The system must gracefully handle failures in LLM calls, file operations, and compliance checks. Appropriate exception handling and fallback mechanisms are expected.
